newsitem.title: FRANCE: France hopes 1997 budget will be its ticket to EMU.
newsitem.headline: France hopes 1997 budget will be its ticket to EMU.

text.p: France's conservative government unveils a spending-cutting 1997 budget on Wednesday which it hopes will underpin the drive to European monetary union by proving it can meet Maastricht standards on budget deficits.

It is widely expected to announce that France's total public deficit will come in at three percent or less of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997, the key year for judging which countries qualify for a single currency when it is launched in 1999.

To reach that goal, it is likely to make deep spending cuts in the central government budget, while also juggling with a range of off-budget revenues to bring the total deficit down from a forecast four percent of GDP this year.

Employment programmes which have failed to create jobs will be axed, as will housing aid subsidies, while some 6,500 to 7,000 civil service posts will be cut through natural wastage, according to government officials.

Altogether, assuming official growth forecasts of 1.3 percent this year and 2.3 percent next year are correct, the 1997 total public deficit will have to be limited to slightly below 250 billion francs ($48.51 billion) -- or three percent of GDP.
Officials refuse to say how they will achieve that while also paying for promised income tax cuts of 25 billion francs.
But they insist that spending will be frozen at 1996 levels. Given inevitable rises on inflation and debt servicing, that implies up to 60 billion francs of cuts elsewhere.
French newspapers say the central government budget deficit may overshoot at around 275 billion francs, including the tax cuts, after 288 billion forecast this year.
To that must be added an expected deficit on France's generous welfare system, which covers healthcare, pensions and family benefits, as well as any local authority deficits.
The government will offset these overshoots to get below the three percent number with off-budget revenues.

These include a transfer of funds from France Telecom to cover future pension liabilities, an accounting surplus from welfare debt repayment fund CADES and a surplus in national unemployment fund UNEDIC.

Economists said that with many details leaked in advance, and with tax cut plans already announced, they expected little to surprise financial markets on Wednesday, but would comb the budget to see how credible the government's plans were.

"Now everybody is expecting a (GDP/deficit ratio) of three percent. The only chance of markets reacting would be if by some fluke they announced 3.2 percent," Marie Owens-Thomsen, chief economist at Banque Internationale de Placement, said. "If they announce 2.9 percent that would be good news."
Economists say France may try to announce a figure below three percent to keep pace with Germany, which last week said it aimed to reduce its deficit to 2.5 percent of GDP next year.
But economists are keen to see evidence of real spending cuts rather than creative accounting to prove France is really headed towards sustainable levels of debt and deficits.
"For this budget to be credible, there have to be cuts in of the running costs of the state," Deutsche Bank economist Patrick Mange said.
He said the risk lay in how well the government was able to implement its planned spending cuts and sustain these through until 1998, when France is due to hold parliamentary elections.

Owens-Thomsen also noted that while France was cutting its deficit, it was piling up big debts, with a debt/GDP ratio nearing the 60 percent ceiling fixed by the Maastricht Treaty -- the economic framework for monetary union.
While France has a relatively low debt/GDP ratio compared to most other European countries, it is moving in the wrong direction, jumping from some 40 percent in 1994.
"Our country is quickly approaching the 60 percent ceiling fixed by the Maastricht treaty," Pierre Joxe, head of the national accounts commission, said on Monday.

"In markets we should worry about direction, not levels. The fact that they are going in the wrong direction on debt is far more worrying than if they only cut the deficit to 3.2 percent," Owens-Thomsen said. ($1=5.154 French Franc)
